explanations.answer: Detest evil and cling to good
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Romans 12:9 says, "Detest what is evil; cling to what is good." Detest is a strong word, and so is cling. I know a little about clinging, because cookie dough has been stuck to my mustache since the Millers' kitchen and it is NOT letting go.

Close in spirit, but the verse asks for more than that. Ignoring evil is a shrug, and admiring good is watching it through the window. Romans 12:9 says, "Detest what is evil; cling to what is good." Detesting and clinging are things you DO, friend.

I see where you're going, but those two words aren't in the verse. Romans 12:9 says, "Detest what is evil; cling to what is good." Detesting evil is a long way from hiding from it. And clinging to good is more than taking notes on it, because you hold on tight with both hands. Or one mustache.

Careful, friend, the verse goes the other way. Romans 12:10 says, "Outdo yourselves in honoring one another." Nobody is told to wait for their turn at the honor. Imagine standing by the oven, arms crossed, waiting for someone else to open the door. Nothing gets baked, and nobody gets honored.

That's right. Romans 12:10 says, "Outdo yourselves in honoring one another." Nobody waits to be honored first. They try to beat each other to it. I'd love to see that race, friend, with everybody sprinting to honor the other guy and nobody left to be honored.

Yes, friend. Romans 12:12 says, "Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer." Hard times are when patience is needed most. Trust me, I know. Sitting in the back of a drawer for years will teach you to wait, whether you like it or not.

Careful is a fine word, but it isn't the one Paul, the apostle writing to Rome, chose here. Romans 12:12 says, "Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer." The hard-times word is patient. Being careful is something you do with a hot tray. Patience is what you do while the batch takes its sweet time.

No silent treatment in this verse, friend. Paul, the apostle writing to Rome, says in Romans 12:12, "Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer." Prayer is the opposite of silence, since you're talking to God. The word for hard times is patient.

That's the one. Romans 12:14 says, "Bless those who persecute you." I know, friend. It's not the first thing anybody wants to do. But there it is in black and white, and the very next line adds, "Bless and do not curse."
I get it, friend, ducking down the other aisle is tempting. But the verse doesn't say that. Romans 12:14 says, "Bless those who persecute you." The command is to bless them, not to dodge them.

That's a reasonable thought, but it isn't what the verse tells them to do. Romans 12:14 says, "Bless those who persecute you. Bless and do not curse." Blessing, not warning, is the word. The verse doesn't hand out lectures here.

You got it, baker. Romans 12:15 says, "Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep." The word is WITH. When a friend is celebrating, you celebrate. When a friend is crying, you sit down and cry beside them. That's what family does.

Nope, friend. Nobody walks up to someone's good news holding a stopwatch and says, "Okay, settle down." Romans 12:15 says, "Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep." You join them where they are.

Sometimes that's kind, but it isn't what this verse says. Romans 12:15 says, "Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep." The word is WITH, friend. Paul wants the believers right there beside the person, feeling it too.

Careful, friend, it's the opposite. Romans 12:16 says, "Do not be proud, but associate with the lowly. Do not be conceited." So no hanging around the important people to look important. The verse points you toward the lowly. It's the whole point.

That's right. Romans 12:16 says, "Live in harmony with one another. Do not be proud, but associate with the lowly. Do not be conceited." No sticking close to the important people. Paul points the believers toward the lowly instead. Friend, you can't be conceited AND hang out with the lowly at the same time.

explanations.answer: As far as it depends on them
explanations.explanation: That's right. Romans 12:18 says, "If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone." The believers do their half, friend. They can't control how the other person acts, and Paul doesn't ask them to. They just make sure peace never fails on their side.

explanations.answer: As long as others apologize first
explanations.explanation: Nice idea, friend, but Paul doesn't say that. Romans 12:18 says, "If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone." The limit is what's possible on THEIR part. Nobody has to stand around waiting for a sorry.

explanations.answer: As long as it feels fair to them
explanations.explanation: I'd like that rule, I'm not gonna lie. But the verse doesn't say it. Romans 12:18 says, "If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone." The limit is whether it's possible on their part, not whether it feels fair.

Yes, friend. Romans 12:19 says, "Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath." Paul backs it up with Scripture: "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord." So the believers put down the scoreboard and leave the paying back to God. It's a lot less tiring that way.

Good try, but leaders aren't in the verse. Romans 12:19 says, "Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath." Then it adds, "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord." The room is left for God.

I see the logic, but the courts don't show up in this verse. Romans 12:19 says, "Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath." It goes on, "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord." The one named is God.

True, friend. Romans 12:20 says, "If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink." Your enemy, the one on the other side of the fight. Feeding him is the opposite of getting even, and it says so right there.

It really does say it, friend. Romans 12:20 says, "If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink." I know. It's not what the human heart reaches for first. But that's what the verse tells them to do.

That's the one, baker. Romans 12:21 says, "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." Evil doesn't get beaten by more evil. It gets beaten by good. A great way to end the whole passage.

Close, but silence isn't the word. Romans 12:21 says, "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." Staying quiet can look like taking it, but Paul wants evil overcome. The tool he names is good.

I get it, you'd think you'd need muscle for that. But Romans 12:21 says, "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." Strength isn't mentioned. Good is the way. I'm a cookie stamper with a mustache, friend, so I'm glad it doesn't take muscle.
